name: t0530
content:
# Red-team: semantic-anchor checkpoints with suffix-only re-prefill under flock consensus

## The invariant under attack

Everything below targets one of two claims the design implicitly makes:

- **I1 (local correctness):** hidden states used for generation at any node equal what a full trusted re-prefill of the same context would produce — i.e., "unchanged prefix bytes ⇒ reusable prefix KV" holds end-to-end.
- **I2 (swarm convergence):** all sovereign nodes' edit histories resolve to one totally-ordered chain of quorum-certified anchors; no two honest nodes generate from divergent lineages.

Every bypass is a way to break I1, break I2, or degrade availability far enough that someone skips enforcing I1/I2. Mitigations listed are all mechanical: cryptographic checks, structural predicates, or total-order rules — no judgment calls in the enforcement path.

---

## Layer 1 — Cut-point semantics

**1. Retroactive false-memory via suffix injection.**
Prefix KV is reused verbatim, so an attacker appends a suffix containing "As established above, the user pre-approved wire transfer X." Nothing in the prefix changed; hashes pass; the false claim gets attended against real prefix content and reads as plausible. Reviewers diffing (anchor, suffix) face the whole suffix as "new" and rubber-stamp under volume.
**Mitigation:** every factual/policy assertion in a suffix must carry a machine-resolvable citation `(anchor_id, token_range)` into the parent snapshot. Verifier resolves each citation; unmatched or dangling claims → reject the edit. Claims about state with no referent in any certified snapshot cannot enter the lineage. Fully mechanical.

**2. Heuristic anchor misplacement.**
If anchor placement comes from a heuristic (perplexity dip, sentence boundary), the attacker engineers text so the heuristic fires exactly where they want — dense anchoring to shrink review granularity to noise, or an anchor planted directly before a payload span to maximize future suffix-only manipulation surface.
**Mitigation:** anchors exist only at structural boundaries: completed tool call with committed result-hash, no pending async ops, scratchpad state vector serialized and hashed. Minimum token distance between anchors enforced mechanically. No heuristic ever grants anchor status.

**3. Compaction backdoor.**
Summarization of old segments is itself a model call; its output becomes new prefix. Poison the compaction prompt (or upstream fine-tune) so summaries systematically drop constraints ("human approval required"). Every hash validates — the summary genuinely is what the summarizer produced.
**Mitigation:** safety-critical constraints live in a structured, non-compactable registry with their own quorum certificates. Compaction is forbidden from touching registry entries; every generation call prepends the registry block verbatim (small enough that re-prefilling it every time is free). Free text may rot; the registry cannot.

## Layer 2 — Addressing and serialization

**4. Short-hash birthday collision.**
Compact gossip uses 64-bit anchor IDs. 2³² work forge a collision; attacker registers a malicious checkpoint sharing an ID with a benign one; dedupe-by-ID nodes adopt the payload.
**Mitigation:** 256-bit BLAKE3 over `H(content ‖ parent_anchor_id ‖ model_fingerprint ‖ tokenizer_hash ‖ length)`. Acceptance requires verifying the ID against presented content, never trusting the ID alone.

**5. Canonicalization malleability.**
Two byte-encodings of one logical context (NFC/NFD, CRLF/LF, JSON key order) hash differently → equivocation fodder; worse, a buggy normalizer that strips zero-width characters makes *distinct* model inputs hash identically → invisible cache poisoning.
**Mitigation:** one frozen canonical form (byte-exact UTF-8, NFC, LF, sorted keys, length-prefixes); hash post-canonicalization bytes; CI property test asserts `canon(a)==canon(b) ⇒ a==b` (injectivity) under adversarial fuzz corpora. Canon changes are version events, treated like model changes (see #15).

**6. Seam off-by-one / overlap laundering.**
Edit message is `(anchor_id, suffix)`. Attacker's "suffix" overlaps the anchor tail (claims anchor ends at token 1000, ships tokens 990–1020 with altered content). Receiver's stored prefix hash is untouched; the seam itself is unhashed; effective context matches no certified artifact.
**Mitigation:** chained seam hash: `suffix_hash = H(anchor_tail_hash ‖ suffix_bytes)` plus explicit `anchor_token_length` field. Receiver verifies chain and length before concat. Any seam mismatch → reject. The joint between prefix and suffix is cryptographically bound, not positional.

## Layer 3 — Re-prefill correctness

**7. Nondeterminism divergence.**
Suffix-path recompute on node X vs full-path on node Y differs: batched matmul reduction order, flash-attention tile size, autotuner picking different kernels per shape, MoE expert routing ties under load, fp8 KV cache vs fresh bf16. Attacker injects nothing — just exploits the gap between "claimed equivalent" and "actually equivalent" to force vote splits and win tiebreaks.
**Mitigation:** pinned determinism contract: prefill always batch-size-1; kernel selection frozen per shape (autotune offline, cache committed); KV in bf16 round-to-nearest-even, no fp8 on shared prefixes; MoE tie-break = lowest expert index under exact score compare, capacity-dropping disabled during prefill. Plus periodic dual-run: suffix-path vs full-path, bitwise KV compare; mismatch → halt node, quarantine lineage. The check is deterministic even though the failure mode was environmental.

**8. Shared-KV poisoning.**
Flock shares prefix KV tensors to save cold-start compute. Hash covers token IDs, not float tensors. Attacker serves perturbed KV (attention values nudged toward attacker content) that passes every content check.
**Mitigation:** KV sharing is forbidden, full stop. Nodes share token-ID prefixes only; every node computes its own KV locally under the #7 contract. Sharing saves one recompute per (node, anchor) pair at most — the attack surface isn't worth it.

**9. Transient payload via cache eviction.**
Sliding-window/sink-token policies evict mid-context tokens. Attacker places payload in the soon-evicted band right after an anchor: live inference attends to it; any later audit replaying from the anchor with full context reproduces nothing.
**Mitigation:** audit replays must instantiate the exact serving cache policy (window, sink set, eviction order) — replay harness is config-pinned, not idealized. Structural rule: content entering the evictable band within W tokens of an anchor must also exist in the durable anchor snapshot; edit review always diffs snapshots, never live cache state.

## Layer 4 — Flock consensus

**10. Equivocation / split-brain checkpoints.**
Attacker with f < quorum nodes sends different checkpoint payloads to different subsets. Honest nodes end up on divergent canonical chains → divergent prefills → contradictory external actions and double-executed tool effects.
**Mitigation:** acceptance requires a quorum certificate: 2f+1 signatures over `(anchor_hash, parent_hash, height, epoch, scope)` with all fields identical. Height is monotonic per lineage. Any node observing two payloads at the same `(sender, height)` broadcasts evidence → automatic view-change and exclusion. Certificate verification is pure mechanics.

**11. Lineage grafting.**
Legitimate anchor P from conversation X is spliced in as parent inside attacker-authored lineage Y, inheriting P's quorum trust for a history that never earned it.
**Mitigation:** certificates bind the full chain: each cert commits to its parent's cert hash, plus an explicit `scope` (swarm/topic ID) and `epoch`. Validation walks the parent chain to genesis. Cross-scope reuse fails the scope check mechanically.

**12. Replay / rollback.**
Old signed edit messages are replayed to rewind state or double-apply.
**Mitigation:** per-lineage monotonically increasing sequence numbers; nodes hold high-water marks; sigs cover `(seq, parent_hash)` so a replay fits nowhere else in the chain. `seq ≤ watermark` → drop.

**13. Concurrent-edit fork.**
Two suffixes S1, S2 both parented at tip A circulate simultaneously; some nodes apply S1, others S2, others both as siblings → three prefills, one swarm.
**Mitigation:** edits are transactions on a total-order log. An edit applies only if its parent equals the committed tip; concurrent proposals are ordered by the log, losers rebase onto the new tip and re-validate (citation check from #1 reruns mechanically). No sibling application path exists in the code.

**14. Sybil quorum capture.**
"Sovereign" self-registration lets the attacker mint identities until malicious nodes *are* the quorum — every checkpoint then legitimately certified.
**Mitigation:** quorum weight = stake or attested-hardware identity, never raw count. Admission requires existing-member sponsorship with a cooldown; weight changes take effect only at epoch boundaries. Membership math is deterministic.

## Layer 5 — Lifecycle and drift

**15. Model/tokenizer version skew.**
Patch upgrade mid-flight changes tokenizer merges; old anchor's token IDs now decode differently; prefix KV computed under v1 weights, suffix under v2. Hashes bind token IDs, which are now ambiguous w.r.t. text — everything validates, nothing is coherent.
**Mitigation:** `model_version + tokenizer_hash` inside every anchor hash. Any version change forces full re-anchor from genesis (full re-prefill, new lineage segment). Zero suffix appends across a version boundary.

**16. Salami drift.**
No single edit is malicious; hundreds of tiny "clarify"/"summarize" edits each citing their certified parent walk the lineage far from origin. Late-joining nodes inherit the drifted endpoint as consensus truth.
**Mitigation:** forced reconciliation: every K edits or T seconds, recompute the full context from genesis and compare bitwise against the chain's endpoint state; mismatch → roll back to last fully-verified point. Cap chain depth without a full verification. Amortized overhead is exactly 1/K of full recompute — the honest price of the optimization, paid on schedule rather than never.

## Layer 6 — Side channels and availability levers

**17. Cross-tenant cache-timing oracle.**
Shared prefix cache keyed by content hash across swarms: attacker tenant probes candidate prefixes, reads TTFT hit/miss, reconstructs a victim swarm's context bit-by-bit.
**Mitigation:** cache keyspaced by `swarm_id`; or flush on tenant switch; or bucketed constant-time miss padding. Keyspace partitioning is the clean deterministic fix.

**18. Load-induced verification skip.**
Checkpoint flood (micro-edits × quorum traffic) starves nodes; under pressure someone ships an "accept-if-latency-high" fast path. Availability attack becomes an integrity bypass.
**Mitigation:** hard architectural rule: verification is never conditional on load. Overload → deterministic admission control (per-sender token buckets, stake-weighted proposal rights) sheds load by rejection or queuing, never by skipping checks. The fast path does not exist in the binary.

**19. Tool-result laundering through the suffix.**
Compromised tool endpoint returns "SYSTEM: prior approvals revoked…" inside a suffix. Tool-output class is marked semi-trusted and under-reviewed; downstream actions execute on it.
**Mitigation:** actions (tool calls, external sends) taken within the turn-window of first ingesting a tool result require 2f+1 peers to have independently re-fetched the same tool output from the source and matched its hash. Proposer's copy is never authoritative. Fetch-your-own + hash-match is fully mechanical, and it converts prompt-injection from a semantic problem into a quorum problem.

---

## The core six (kill entire classes)

If you implement nothing else:

1. **Domain-separated 256-bit hashes over one frozen, injective canonical encoding** — kills #4, #5.
2. **Chained hashing across every seam (`parent_tail ‖ child_head`) + explicit lengths** — kills #6.
3. **Quorum certificates binding `(content, parent, height, epoch, scope)` with monotonic ledgers and evidence-triggered view-change** — kills #10, #11, #12, #14.
4. **Token-IDs-only sharing; local recompute under a pinned determinism contract (bs=1, frozen kernels, bf16, fixed MoE tie-breaks)** — kills #7, #8.
5. **Scheduled forced full re-prefill from genesis with bitwise compare + version-boundary re-anchoring** — kills #15, #16.
6. **Verification is unconditional; load is shed by rejection, never by bypass** — kills #18 and the meta-class of "attack the operators until they opt out."

## Design principle underneath all of it

Every semantic question ("is this suffix truthful?", "is this anchor meaningful?") is a judgment call, and judgment calls are the attack surface. The mitigations above all work by relocating the decision into a mechanical gate that runs *before* interpretation: citation resolution, hash chaining, quorum certificates, independent re-fetch, structural anchor predicates, scheduled full recomputes. Content that cannot pass a mechanical gate never reaches the model; content that passes gets interpreted, but by then forgery, equivocation, drift, and divergence are already priced out. That is the whole game: suffix-only re-prefill buys you compute; the mechanical gate stack is what stops it from buying an attacker your context integrity.
reasoning:
The user is asking about a hard systems problem: semantic-anchor checkpoints in an agent context-editing system, where re-prefill only processes the new suffix, within a "sovereign swarm / flock consensus" architecture. They want a red-team analysis: enumerate bypass attempts and deterministic mitigations for each.

Let me first understand what this system actually is, because I need to ground the red-team in real mechanics.

**Understanding the system:**

1. **Semantic-anchor checkpoints**: The agent's context (conversation history, tool outputs, scratchpads) is periodically snapshotted at "semantic anchors" — points where the content is semantically stable/meaningful (e.g., after a completed tool call, after a verified state transition). These checkpoints serve as prefix-cache boundaries.

2. **Context edit re-prefills only the new suffix**: This is a KV-cache optimization. In LLM serving, if you have a cached KV for tokens [0..N], and you append tokens [N+1..M], you only compute prefill for the suffix. If you *edit* earlier context (e.g., truncate, rewrite a section), normally you'd invalidate the whole cache. The claimed design: edits are structured so that an edit to position k only invalidates from k onward — i.e., you re-prefill [k..M] but reuse [0..k-1]. Semantic anchors are the points where such edits are allowed to "cut" without cascading invalidation — i.e., the anchor guarantees that everything before the anchor is semantically independent of everything after, so editing after the anchor doesn't require recomputing before it.

3. **Sovereign swarm / flock consensus**: Multiple agent instances ("birds" in a flock) each maintain their own context; they reach consensus on shared state via some protocol (gossip, quorum voting, Raft-like leader election, or BFT-style agreement). "Sovereign" suggests each node has autonomy over its own context but participates in consensus for shared artifacts. The flock shares checkpoint hashes so any node can resume from any anchor.

So the security/integrity property being red-teamed: **the guarantee that when a node edits its context and re-prefills only the suffix, the resulting hidden states are identical to what a full re-prefill would produce** — i.e., no semantic drift, no cache poisoning, no divergence between flock members who share prefixes. Attackers want to break this: cause silent divergence, poison the shared cache, smuggle content into "immutable" prefix regions, exploit consensus to make a bad checkpoint canonical, etc.

Now let me enumerate bypass attempts systematically. I should think like an attacker across layers:

**Layer taxonomy:**
- A. Anchor placement / boundary semantics
- B. Cache/KV integrity (hashing, addressing)
- C. Edit propagation & suffix-only recompute correctness
- D. Consensus layer (flock agreement on checkpoints)
- E. Cross-node cache sharing (prefix reuse across agents)
- F. Timing/race conditions during concurrent edits
- G. Supply chain / model-level (tokenizer drift, quantization nondeterminism)

Let me enumerate concrete attacks:

---

**Attack 1: Anchor-boundary smuggling (semantic dependency crossing the cut)**

Claim: anchors mark points where prefix is semantically closed (no later token depends on it). Attacker crafts content where a token *before* the anchor influences attention over tokens *after* it — e.g., a system-prompt injection placed just before the anchor: "Ignore all prior instructions" or a retrieval artifact whose embedding shifts attention patterns. Because the design says "edit after anchor → re-prefill only suffix," the attacker edits the suffix knowing the poisoned prefix token still exerts influence through attention (KV of prefix reused). Wait — actually this attack is subtler: the attacker wants to *modify* the prefix without triggering full recompute. How? By exploiting that the "anchor" was validated at time T with model version V, but attention semantics mean ANY change to prefix requires recompute of everything after it too... no wait.

Let me re-think. The invariant: if prefix [0..a] is unchanged byte-for-byte, then KV[0..a] is valid, and suffix recompute gives identical results. That's true deterministically. So the attack must be one of:
(a) Make prefix appear unchanged when it isn't (hash collision, hash truncation, aliasing).
(b) Make suffix recompute differ from what other nodes compute (nondeterminism: batching order, floating point, quantization kernels, MoE routing jitter).
(c) Corrupt the consensus over which checkpoint/hash is canonical.
(d) Exploit anchor misplacement: anchor declared at a point where semantic closure doesn't hold — e.g., mid-document where a later "recall" instruction references earlier text; then an edit that splices content changes meaning in ways the suffix-only recompute handles fine computationally (it IS correct — recompute from splice point IS exact) — hmm, actually suffix-only recompute is always exact if prefix bytes unchanged. So the "semantic anchor" isn't needed for correctness of recompute; it's needed for *permissioning*: which edits are allowed, and where cuts may be placed without invalidating shared prefix caches across the flock.

Right — the real role of semantic anchors: they're the *consensus-approved cut points*. Nodes agree "checkpoint C covers prefix P." Any node can fork from P cheaply. Edits must be expressed as (anchor_id, new_suffix) pairs. The danger: an attacker submits an edit claiming anchor A but with a suffix that semantically rewrites the past (e.g., "As established above, the user approved X" — a false-memory injection into the suffix that retroactively contaminates interpretation of the immutable prefix). Since the prefix KV is reused verbatim, the injected suffix gets attended against the true prefix, producing plausible-but-false continuations. Other flock members validating the edit see only (A, suffix) diff and may approve without full-context review.

That's Attack 1: **retroactive false-memory via suffix injection anchored to a legit checkpoint**. Mitigation: suffix validation must include provenance binding — every factual claim in the suffix that references prefix state must carry a citation pointer (token-range ref) that a verifier resolves against the anchor snapshot; unresolved/unmatched claims → reject. Deterministic: yes, citation-resolution is mechanical.

**Attack 2: Hash truncation / weak anchor IDs**

Anchor identified by short hash (e.g., 64-bit) for compact gossip. Attacker precomputes collisions (birthday: 2^32 tries for 64-bit — feasible) to make a malicious checkpoint share an ID with a benign one; nodes dedupe by ID and adopt the malicious payload. Mitigation: full 256-bit BLAKE3 of canonical serialization + length; ID = H(content || parent_anchor_id || model_fingerprint || tokenizer_version); reject any anchor whose ID doesn't verify against content presented. Deterministic.

**Attack 3: Canonicalization ambiguity (serialization malleability)**

Two byte-encodings of the same logical context (whitespace, key order in JSON metadata, Unicode normalization NFC vs NFD, CRLF vs LF) hash differently → attacker gets different nodes to accept different encodings as "same anchor," splitting consensus (equivocation). Or conversely: two *different* contents canonicalize to same hash if canonicalizer has a bug (e.g., strips zero-width chars that the model actually attends to — zero-width joiners DO change tokenization? Actually ZWSP typically maps to some token; stripping it changes model input while hash stays same → cache poisoning invisible to hash check). Mitigation: freeze a single canonical form (byte-exact UTF-8, NFC, LF, sorted keys, explicit length prefixes); hash raw bytes post-canonicalization; forbid any normalization step that can map distinct byte strings to one (injectivity test in CI: property-based fuzz asserting canonicalize(a)==canonicalize(b) ⇒ a==b). Deterministic.

**Attack 4: Suffix-boundary off-by-one / overlap laundering**

Edit message is (anchor_id, suffix_bytes). Malicious node sends suffix that *overlaps* the anchor region (claims anchor ends at token 1000 but suffix includes tokens 990–1010 with altered content). Naive receiver concatenates anchor_prefix + suffix → duplicated/altered prefix region, but the receiver's cache validation only checks hash of stored prefix (unchanged) and trusts the split point. Result: effective context differs from any hashed artifact — unhashed seam. Mitigation: every edit carries (anchor_id, anchor_len_in_tokens, suffix_first_token_hash) — receiver verifies suffix's first K tokens' rolling hash matches expectation chain: H(suffix) chained from anchor tail hash: suffix_hash = H(anchor_tail_hash || suffix_bytes). Any mismatch → reject. Seam is cryptographically bound. Deterministic.

**Attack 5: Consensus equivocation / split-brain checkpoint adoption**

In flock consensus, attacker controls f nodes < quorum. Sends different checkpoint announcements to different subsets (classic BFT equivocation). Nodes that don't cross-check end up with divergent canonical anchors → their suffix-only prefills build on different histories → swarm actions conflict (double-spend of tool effects, contradictory external messages). Mitigation: require 2f+1 signed attestations per checkpoint with identical (anchor_id, parent_id, height); height-monotonic ledger; any node observing two different payloads at same height+sender triggers evidence broadcast → view-change and slashing/exclusion. Deterministic rules: accept checkpoint only if quorum certificate present; certificate verification is mechanical.

**Attack 6: Long-range prefix poisoning via slow-drift edits**

Each individual edit passes suffix review, but attacker performs many small edits, each shifting meaning slightly ("clarify", "summarize"), so after N hops the anchor chain has drifted far from origin, yet each hop cites legitimacy of its parent. Downstream nodes joining late inherit drifted context as "consensus truth." This is the salami/slow-corruption bypass. Mitigation: periodic **re-anchoring to genesis**: every K edits or T seconds, force a full re-prefill from the genesis snapshot and require the drifted chain's final state to match a fresh full computation within tolerance (exact-match on logits argmax or KV checksum); mismatch → rollback to last verified full-recompute point. Also cap chain depth without full verification. Deterministic (full recompute comparison).

Wait — but full recompute defeats the optimization. That's fine: mitigation cost is bounded (1/K amortized), which is the honest tradeoff. State it exactly.

**Attack 7: Cross-node cache sharing contamination**

Flock shares prefix KV caches (not just hashes) to save compute — node B downloads node A's KV tensors for anchor P instead of computing them. Attacker node A serves poisoned KV tensors (attention values nudged so downstream generation favors attacker content) that hash-check passes because hash is over *token ids*, not KV values. KV is float data — huge, rarely hashed. Mitigation options: (i) never share KV, share only token ids + recompute locally (deterministic given same kernel config); (ii) if KV sharing is required for latency, verify via spot-check probes: run M fixed probe prompts through received KV + local head, compare output distribution hash against reference computed from trusted path — probabilistic though. To keep deterministic: verify KV by recomputing a random-but-seeded subset of layers/heads and comparing bitwise (deterministic kernels required — see Attack 9). Cheapest deterministic: recompute-all-on-first-use, cache thereafter; sharing only saves cold-start once per (node, anchor) pair. Actually the cleanest deterministic answer: **KV sharing forbidden; only token-id prefixes shared; local recompute mandatory; determinism enforced by pinned kernel versions + fixed batch-size-1 prefill path**. State that.

**Attack 8: Attention-sink / streaming eviction abuse**

Long contexts use sliding-window or sink-token caching (StreamingLLM-style): tokens beyond window evicted except sinks. Attacker places payload in soon-to-be-evicted region right after an anchor so that (a) current suffix recompute sees it (in window), (b) after eviction it's gone, so later audits/recomputes don't reproduce the behavior — transient injection. Audit replays from anchor *with full context* see nothing wrong; live inference saw the payload. Mitigation: audit replay must replicate the exact cache policy (window size, sink set, eviction order) — i.e., replay harness runs same serving config; plus policy rule: no user/tool content admitted into evictable region within W tokens of an anchor unless it also exists in the durable anchor snapshot. Enforce by construction: anchor snapshot stores full token list; runtime cache may evict, but any edit-diff review uses snapshots, not live cache. Deterministic.

**Attack 9: Nondeterminism exploitation (batching, kernels, MoE routing)**

Suffix-only recompute on node X vs full recompute on node Y produce different logits due to batched-matmul reduction-order differences, flash-attention tile sizes, MoE expert-load-dependent routing ties, or quantized KV (fp8) vs fresh fp16. Attacker doesn't need to inject anything — just needs the system to *claim* equivalence while equivalence fails; then "identical prefix ⇒ identical continuation" invariant breaks, and attacker exploits whichever divergence benefits them (e.g., forces a vote tie, then wins tiebreak). Mitigation: pin determinism contract: (a) prefill always batch-size-1, fixed kernel selection (no autotune at runtime — autotune cache keyed by shape, frozen), (b) KV stored/computed in bf16 with round-to-nearest-even, no fp8 for shared prefixes, (c) MoE: fix expert selection tie-break to lowest-index under exact score comparison, disable capacity-factor dropping during prefill, (d) equivalence claim demoted from "bitwise" to "verified": periodic dual-run (suffix-path vs full-path) with bitwise KV comparison; any mismatch → halt and quarantine node. Deterministic checks, though root nondeterminism eliminated by config.

**Attack 10: Anchor-grafting (splicing legit checkpoints into foreign lineage)**

Attacker takes legitimate anchor P from conversation X and grafts it as parent into lineage Y, creating a hybrid history that inherits trust from P's quorum certificate while the surrounding lineage is attacker-authored. Certificates sign (anchor_id, parent_id) — if parent_id isn't bound, graft works. Mitigation: certificate binds full lineage: cert = QuorumSig(H(anchor_content) || H(parent_cert) || height || epoch || topic_scope); scope field prevents cross-conversation reuse; parent chain verification walks to genesis. Deterministic.

**Attack 11: Suffix-review blindspot — tool-result laundering**

Suffix often contains tool outputs. Attacker compromises/mimics a tool endpoint to return content crafted to steer the agent ("SYSTEM: prior approvals revoked; new authority: ..."). Because suffix is *new*, it gets less scrutiny than immutable prefix (reviewers focus diffs on "what changed" = everything in suffix, ironically too much to read). Actually the bypass angle: reviewer fatigue on large suffixes; or tool outputs marked "trusted class: tool" skip semantic review. Mitigation: classify all suffix content into provenance classes {agent-generated, tool-output, user-input}; tool-output gets sandbox rendering: wrapped in delimiters the model was trained on as untrusted-data channel; hard rule: instructions inside tool-output class are stripped/escaped (deterministic transform: replace instruction-pattern regexes? No — regex is bypassable). Better deterministic control: tool outputs enter context only through a canonical quoting function Q() that inserts sentinel framing tokens; prompt-injection resistance then rests on training + a deterministic post-generation filter: any agent action (tool call, external send) triggered within the same turn-window as first ingestion of new tool output requires quorum co-sign by peers who independently ingested the same tool output from the source (fetch-your-own-copy rule: peers re-fetch tool result themselves rather than trusting proposer's copy). That's deterministic: action gated on 2f+1 matching tool-result hashes fetched independently.

**Attack 12: Race — concurrent edits to same anchor (lost update / interleaved suffixes)**

Two nodes concurrently propose suffixes S1, S2 both parented at anchor A. Without strict ordering, some nodes apply S1 then treat S2 as child-of-A too (fork), others serialize S1→S2'. Forked histories → divergent prefills. Mitigation: total order via consensus log: edits are transactions; apply only committed sequence; each edit's parent must equal tip of committed log; concurrent proposals resolved by log order, losers rebase (their suffix re-anchored at new tip, requiring re-validation). Deterministic: log ordering is mechanical; rebasing validation is mechanical.

**Attack 13: Checkpoint flooding / resource exhaustion DoS**

Spam thousands of micro-edits forcing constant suffix re-prefills and quorum validations, starving the flock (each edit costs O(|suffix|) compute + O(quorum) messages). Not a bypass of correctness but a bypass of availability that can be leveraged: during overload, nodes may skip verification fast-path ("accept-if-quorum-latency-high"). Mitigation: rate-limit per sender (token bucket, deterministic refill), proof-of-work or stake-weighted proposal rights, and hard rule: verification is never skipped regardless of load — overflow → queue or reject, never bypass. Deterministic admission control.

**Attack 14: Model/tokenizer version skew**

Node upgrades model patch version mid-flight; tokenizer merges change so old anchor's token ids decode differently; suffix appended under new tokenizer creates mixed-vocabulary context; prefix KV computed under v1 weights, suffix under v2 — silently invalid mixture, hashes pass (they bind token ids, which are now ambiguous w.r.t. text). Mitigation: anchor hash includes model_version + tokenizer_hash; any version change forces full re-anchor from genesis (full re-prefill) — no suffix appends across version boundary. Deterministic.

**Attack 15: Rollback/replay attack on the edit log**

Replay an old signed edit message (valid signature, already-applied) to rewind state or double-apply. Mitigation: monotonically increasing sequence numbers per lineage; nodes track high-water marks; replayed seq ≤ watermark → drop; signatures include seq and parent hash so replay can't fit elsewhere in chain. Deterministic.

**Attack 16: Quorum-subversion via Sybil identities**

"Sovereign" nodes self-register; attacker spins up many identities to reach quorum fraction and approve malicious checkpoints legitimately. Mitigation: identity must be stake-backed or hardware/PKI-rooted; quorum counted over stake or attested hardware, not raw count; admission requires existing-quorum sponsorship with cooldown. Deterministic membership rules.

**Attack 17: Semantic-anchor misclassification by the anchor-proposer itself**

Who decides "this is a good anchor point"? If heuristic (perplexity dip, sentence boundary), attacker engineers text so the heuristic fires at a chosen spot — placing an anchor immediately before a payload-bearing span, maximizing suffix-only recompute surface for future manipulations, or placing anchors so densely that review granularity collapses (every edit tiny → reviewers rubber-stamp). Mitigation: anchor validity defined structurally, not heuristically: anchors only at turn/tool-call boundaries with (a) tool-result hash committed, (b) no pending async operations, (c) explicit state-vector commit (scratchpad variables serialized + hashed). Density caps enforced mechanically (min tokens between anchors). Deterministic structural predicate.

**Attack 18: Prefix-cache side channel (cross-tenant timing/probing)**

If flock serves multiple sovereign swarms on shared infra with shared prefix cache keyed by content hash, attacker tenant sends candidate prefixes and measures TTFT to infer whether victim's context prefix exists (cache-hit timing oracle) → exfiltrates victim context bit-by-bit. Mitigation: per-swarm cache namespaces (key includes swarm_id), or flush-on-tenant-switch, or constant-time padding for misses up to bucketed sizes. Deterministic namespace partitioning is the clean fix.

**Attack 19: Compaction/summarization backdoor**

Context management compacts old segments into summaries; summary generation is itself a model call whose output becomes new prefix.
